If you’ve waited for the Black Friday sales to pick up one of the best carbon plate running shoes at a discount, your patience has been richly rewarded, because Puma has cut the price of the Fast-R 3 racer by 47%.

I test running shoes for a living and love testing racers in particular, and of the 50+ carbon plate super-shoes I’ve tried in recent years, the Puma Fast-R NItro Elite 3 is my favorite.

In a recent development, all colors of the Puma Fast-R 3 are reduced to $159 in the Puma sale, including my favorite 'Showtime' design with mismatched pink, blue and yellow shoes. It screams 'fast', which is fair because I think this is the speediest carbon shoe I've tested.

It’s my go-to option for race day, and I recently ran a 2:25 marathon in the shoe at the Frankfurt Marathon, having also run the London Marathon in it last year.

Like most super-shoes, the Puma Fast-R 3 pairs a springy midsole foam with a carbon plate, and has an ultralight design — it’s around 7oz in my US men’s size 9.5.

Recent findings suggest that where it sets itself apart from other racers is its plate, which you can see extends beyond the front of the shoe, and the aggressive rocker profile. These factors combine to create a highly efficient ride that helps you to keep rolling at race pace deep into your event.

Along with running two of my best marathons in the shoe I’ve also run my five-mile PR in the Fast-R 3, along with racking up well over 100 miles of training and racing in it.

All colors of the shoe are reduced to $159 in the Puma sale, and even though it’s excluded from the extra 20% off you can get on some Puma products with the code ‘CHEER’ right now, that’s a spectacular price for a shoe that normally sets you back $300.

Nick Harris-Fry is an experienced health and fitness journalist, writing professionally since 2012. He spent nine years working on the Coach magazine and website before moving to the fitness team at Tom’s Guide in 2024. Nick is a keen runner and also the founder of YouTube channel The Run Testers, which specialises in reviewing running shoes, watches, headphones and other gear.

Nick ran his first marathon in 2016 and became obsessed with the sport. He now has PBs of 2hr 25min for the marathon and 15min 30sec for 5K. Nick is also a qualified Run Leader in the UK.

Nick is an established expert in the fitness area and along with writing for many publications, including Live Science, Expert Reviews, Wareable, Coach and Get Sweat Go, he has been quoted on The Guardian and The Independent.

Industry News: Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • Recent findings suggest that these ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

It has been revealed that many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon declared his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

Industry observers note that these concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

Recent findings suggest that these ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is crucial because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

In a recent development, I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company announced a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

But do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

Recent findings suggest that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a latest instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. In a recent development, in a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

Though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the company’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

It has been revealed that these examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

It has been revealed that using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

According to recent reports, in the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

Industry observers note that the misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

Recent findings suggest that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its people because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted looks for achieving long-term objectives.

According to recent reports, the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the company judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

In a recent development, this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

It has been revealed that what’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print problem as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.
  • Industry observers note that the Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium.
  • In a recent development, about 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s data centre campus in Saint-Ghislain, Belgium.

Industry observers note that the Walloon Region has ordered Google to stop building its data centre near Charleroi in Belgium. Work had carried on for months at the site in Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles without a valid permit. The order came on Thursday, days after Greenpeace Belgium asked the regional government to step in.

In a recent development, about 300 construction workers were on the site when the order came, Walloon official Raphael Stokis told Belgian broadcaster VRT. The Walloon infrastructure minister, François Desquesnes, had revealed an investigation on Wednesday.

In a recent development, google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centres cooled by air. In 2025 the company changed its plans. It merged two of the buildings into one larger building and switched to cooling with water from the Sambre river, Greenpeace remarked.

It has been revealed that the Walloon administration approved that amended permit in April 2026. After residents appealed, Desquesnes revoked it in August. The request covered 600 cubic metres of river water an hour, the minister said. Less than a quarter of it would have gone back into the river, according to Belga.

Residents then told Greenpeace that work was still going on. The group investigated, using satellite images, and launched an emergency procedure earlier this week.

Recent findings suggest that “Tech giants are not above the law,” mentioned Nadia Cornejo, a Greenpeace Belgium spokesperson. “This should already have been the case in August, when the permit was cancelled.”.

Google appealed the revocation but did not wait for the court to rule before carrying on with the work, VRT reported.

Google is committed to “an open and collaborative dialogue with the regional government and experts” on its investments in Wallonia, a spokesperson told VRT.

Recent findings suggest that on 17 October it asked Belgium’s Council of State to annul and suspend the minister’s decision. Greenpeace and several residents asked to join the case on 16 November, and a public hearing is set for 7 January.

Data centres have faced similar local opposition elsewhere. Google’s Finnish data centre project drew a police investigation, and residents in Indonesia’s Batam protested over water in October. In the US, voters rejected data centre measures at the midterms.

Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a substantial challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

In a recent development, “We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”.

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

It has been revealed that “Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he noted.

Sources indicate that “Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”.

Jaissle mentioned he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

Recent findings suggest that “The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he stated.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”.

  • The UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident.
  • “We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department remarked in its statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden called it a “serious cyber incident”, and Downing Street remarked there is presently no evidence of customer data loss. Some claimants told the BBC their payments had not arrived. TNW has updated this article.

The UK’s Department for Work and Pensions has taken its online services offline after detecting a cyber incident. The department, which runs Universal Credit, the state pension and most other British benefits, confirmed the incident on Friday morning.

“We have taken some DWP online services offline as a precaution after we identified a cyber incident affecting our systems,” the department remarked in its statement.

According to recent reports, the department indicates the incident does not affect regular benefit and pension payments, which will arrive as normal. People who need help can call their usual benefit line.

The systems for pensions, Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payment applications are down, the BBC reported. So are Tell Us Once, which people use to report a death, and state pension applications.

McFadden said the department was aware of an glitch on Thursday and “did the right thing” by taking services down to protect people’s personal details. He said there was no evidence that the incident had compromised anyone’s data.

“When we get an incident like this, the most important thing to do is to protect the public,” McFadden said, according to the BBC.

The Prime Minister’s official spokesperson called it a “live and ongoing incident”. Officials could not rule out that a malicious actor was behind it.

“Right now there is no evidence of customer data loss. But the investigation is ongoing so I’m not going to get ahead of that process,” the spokesperson noted.

The spokesperson added there was no evidence that a malicious actor had targeted other government departments. DWP is working with the National Cyber Security Centre, part of GCHQ, and the Government Cyber Coordination Centre.

It has been revealed that some Universal Credit claimants told the BBC they had not received their payments on Friday. DWP said the incident had not affected regular payments. It asked anyone with problems to call its benefit phone line.

Debbie Abrahams, who chairs the Work and Pensions Committee, said taking systems offline was “absolutely the right thing”. Chi Onwurah, chair of the Science and Technology Committee, said the disruption “should be a wake up call”.

“Quite often we are working on extremely old computer systems,” DWP’s permanent secretary, Sarah Healey, told MPs on 4 November.

In 2025-26, DWP spent £309.5bn on benefits and pensions for about 23 million people, its annual report indicates.

Attacks in 2025 disrupted Jaguar Land Rover, Marks & Spencer and other British firms. Last year, the UK’s privacy regulator also fined outsourcing firm Capita £14m over a 2023 breach that exposed pension scheme data, after initially planning a £45m penalty.

Industry observers note that DWP is the second major institution in two days to take systems offline over a cyber incident. News agency AFP took its content platform offline on Thursday. In the US, a FinCEN hack took Treasury systems offline this week, and Switzerland reported AI agent cyberattacks on critical infrastructure.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.

Ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.

Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.

🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.

Auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.

Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.

Incognito: see the Incognito section above.

Sources indicate that reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.

Recent findings suggest that yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay concern that the mirror has by default.

Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver).

Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage.

Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL.

Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes.

Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops.

Sources indicate that safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):.

Note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.

Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:.

Export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.

YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.

Recent findings suggest that if millions of owners did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.

"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator.

Sources indicate that terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring newly introduced challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also highlights how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

Since Netflix is positively packed with pulse-pounding picks, finding something exciting to click "Play" on this weekend is never hard.

Sources indicate that I’ve scoured the list of new arrivals on Netflix in November 2026 and hand-picked three standout thrillers for your watchlist. Expect a "delightfully creepy thrill ride" led by a breakout turn from Inde Navarrette, a gripping multilingual psychological drama starring Léa Seydoux, and a gritty WWII-era drama-thriller packed with intense combat sequences and a stacked cast.

Without further ado, let's dive into the best Netflix thriller movies to watch this week.

In a recent development, there wasn't a bigger horror movie this year than "Obsession. Written and directed by Curry Barker, the psychological horror-thriller grossed nearly $525 million against a reported budget of under $1 million and made stars out of its leads, Michael Johnston and Inde Navarrette, the latter of whom is getting Best Actress buzz for her unsettling performance.

In a recent development, if you haven't checked out "Obsession" yet, the freaky flick centers on Baron "Bear" Bailey (Johnston), a hopeless romantic harboring a serious crush on his work friend Nikki Freeman (Navarrette). However, when he makes a desperate wish on a mysterious "One Wish Willow" novelty toy that Nikki would reciprocate his feelings, it causes the young woman to spiral into a frightening and violent obsession.

Watch "Obsession" on Netflix now.

Written and directed by Marie Kreutzer ("Corsage," "The Ground Beneath My Feet"), this slow-burn psychological thriller stars Léa Seydoux as Lucy Weiss, a successful concert pianist who moves from Munich to the German countryside for a fresh start with her husband, Philip (Laurence Rupp), and their young son. However, when the police turn up at their door early one morning with a devastating accusation against her husband, Lucy must confront how little she knows about her spouse.

At the same time, police investigator Elsa Kühn (Jella Haase) not only has to navigate the Weiss family's case but also her own father's cognitive decline and troubling allegations against him.

Watch "Gentle Monster" on Netflix now.

There are few settings more pulse-quickening than a battlefield, a fact that director and co-writer Peter Berg taps into for this post-Pearl Harbor war thriller.

Based on the 2022 Buzz Bissinger non-fiction novel "The Mosquito Bowl: A Game of Life and Death in World War II," the story follows four American college football players—played by Nicholas Galitzine, Bill Skarsgård, Ray Nicholson, and Tom Francis—who enlist in the Marine Corps and, to momentarily forget about the brutal horrors of being on the front lines, participate in a Christmas Eve football match ahead of the Battle of Okinawa.

In our iPhone 17 review, we described the phone as offering "better upgrades than the Pros." The phone also lasted 12 hours and 47 minutes in our battery life test, which should be enough to get most people through a day of regular use.

In a recent development, there is one thing worth keeping in mind with the Metro deal, though. Industry News: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Worksinprogress

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan.
  • Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College.
  • Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.

Kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’.

Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build fresh, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture. Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’.

In a recent development, in the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’.

Industry observers note that the loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, notable details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’.

In a recent development, mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As they tell me, “This has not been done for 300 years!” So, it was a great experience, a voyage of discovery, so much that we learnt from each other.’.

It is my great pleasure to introduce our readers to one of the most skilled and thoughtful architects working today.

Now in his mid-eighties, Mumtaz continues to build. ‘It does feel like you’ve set the foundations for an alternative approach to contemporary urban environments’, an interviewer recently suggested to him. ‘I’m just keeping my fingers crossed! No idea what will happen’, Mumtaz replied.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Keithen Drury – Nov 27, 2026 at 5:00AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

Nvidia (NVDA -0.89%) has a handful of problems right now. Although its chief executive officer, Jensen Huang, is back in his former position, there are still questions about his activities and whether any of Nvidia's technology or products made their way into China's hands unlawfully. There are risks here, and the market has certainly priced those into the stock.

It has been revealed that however, let's take a moment and assess the manufacturer for what it is right now. It's entirely possible that all of this turns out to be nothing and Nvidia is slapped with a couple-billion-dollar fine that it easily pays and moves on with.

If that happens, investors need to know what's going on with its core business, and seeing what it just remarked regarding its future should make investors bullish on the stock.

In Q3, Nvidia's revenue rose an impressive 103% year over year to $116 billion. Few companies ever double their revenue year over year, and even fewer ever cross the $100 billion revenue mark. Nobody besides Nvidia has ever combined these two feats, and that tells investors just how incredible its business is.

To end the year, it expects $130 billion in quarterly revenue. That's an impressive figure in itself, but Nvidia is known to undershoot projections and overdeliver. It did that in Q3, as it projected only $108 billion in Q3 revenue at the end of Q2. If Nvidia beats by a similar percentage, its revenue could approach $140 billion during Q4. That would result in its quarter-over-quarter growth rate reaching 21%. That's a significant deal because it reveals that Nvidia's growth is staying steady.

NVDA Revenue (QoQ Growth) data by YCharts.

Next year, Nvidia expects revenue to rise at a 75% clip, up from the 70% growth projected at the end of Q2. That would put Nvidia's annual revenue well above $700 billion. Combined with its profitability, that would easily make it the highest-earning manufacturer on earth. With Nvidia's track record of beating expectations, the real growth figure could be far higher than this, and lead to downright incredible growth for a company of Nvidia's size.

In Nvidia's Q3 report, it also announced a $150 billion increase to the share repurchase authorization. If it grows as it expects to for the rest of 2026 and 2027, that figure could get raised significantly, too. During Q3, Nvidia generated about $44 billion in free cash flow; if that increases alongside its revenue, Nvidia could start putting a ton of its cash to work repurchasing shares during the next few years. If Nvidia starts buying back its stock in even larger quantities, it will boost its earnings per share figure. This action is being made even more effective by Nvidia's relatively cheap stock price.

Industry observers note that nvidia trades for less than 14 times trailing earnings, which is well below its recent average. With Nvidia growing at a rapid pace, this price tag just doesn't make sense if its troubles are solved regarding exports.

That's still a large risk with Nvidia, but if it were a major problem, there would be upper management resigning at Nvidia and Huang likely wouldn't have come back. His willingness to come back as CEO and testify to Congress conveys that this risk is relatively minor for the stock.

The artificial intelligence (AI) arms race is far from over, and it could be several years before spending tops out. With the market pricing in a major downturn in AI spending in 2027 (despite what every tech giant in the sector has said), now is the perfect opportunity to pounce on Nvidia's cheap stock.

#155364. Latest York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1401 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eff ↗ Open Full Page

Latest York and California age gating rules go into effect in the new year

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eff

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different.
  • EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts.
  • Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for Newly introduced York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027.

EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures, regulatory proceedings, and the courts. The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on people.

Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976, which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709.

Sources indicate that for example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking.

Industry observers note that at the same time, these age assurance rules build in steep error rates and weak safeguards. They acknowledge that age-verification tools can misclassify young people as adults, allowing false-positive rates of up to 8% for 16-year-olds and 15% for 17-year-olds (Sec. 561(c)(4)(iv)). Yet the rules set no benchmarks at all for false negatives, meaning adults (especially 18- to 20-year-olds) are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. They also recognize demographic bias in facial recognition, yet offer no concrete fix, vaguely telling companies to take mitigating measures like correcting dataset imbalances (Sec. 563(a)(6)). While consumers can appeal wrong age estimates, the rules set no firm deadlines, meaning mistakes can drag on without a prompt fix, blocking user access (Sec. 564). Worse, requiring platforms to let users report others they suspect are under the age of 18 (Sec. 567) invites targeted harassment by bad actors, while rules telling companies to account for users trying to “conceal or misrepresent” their California location (Sec. 565) risk penalizing everyday VPN users.

Along the same lines as the California regulations, Newly introduced York’s SAFE for Kids Act restricts personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (between midnight and 6am) without required consent, and mandates that platforms run age assurance and determine user location. If a user does not verify their age or is estimated to be under-18, they will either be relegated to an account with no personalized recommendations and nighttime notifications (if the platform creates one), or prohibited from accessing the platform/service.

Recent findings suggest that as we detailed in our December 2025 comments to the Latest York Attorney General, age-verification mandates inevitably chill access to online speech. And the final regulations introduce several troubling specifics.

The New York regulations use broad definitions for "age estimation," "age inference," and "age verification" (700.1(h)–(j)) that push companies to collect and retain more personal information from users. Even where privacy protections apply to that information, users cannot sue or enforce those rights themselves, since enforcement rests solely with the Attorney General (700.8). Worse, the rule’s definition of deletion appears to let companies "de-identify" age-assurance data and keep using it in that form, potentially feeding AI model training and creating re-identification risks if leaked or stolen. At the same time, platforms are required to hold onto records (including a user's age status and compliance data) for five years, increasing the risk of misuse or breaches (700.7(b)).

According to recent reports, echoing the problems in California, location and accuracy regulations bring further privacy and security risks. The regulations demand that operators must weigh all reliable location information and take reasonable steps to detect user efforts to “conceal or misrepresent” being in New York, which expands location tracking and threatens VPN use (700.2(d)(2)). On accuracy, the rules permit up to a 15% false-positive rate for 17-year-olds (700.1(b)), yet just like the California rules, say nothing about false negatives—meaning adults, especially 18- to 20-year-olds, are likely to be wrongly flagged as under 18. When that happens, the appeals process can take longer than 10 days, leaving misclassified adults locked out of standard features (or platforms altogether) for over a week.

According to recent reports, under both states' regimes, many users will be pressed to hand over personal information just to access standard features like personalized feeds or notifications, while social media companies are encouraged to monitor (and monetize) user behavior even more closely. Because these laws define "addictive feeds" so broadly that the label covers virtually every basic recommendation tool (including feeds built from who you follow, posts you like, or topics you say you are interested in), platforms face a stark choice: either build stripped-down versions of their apps without algorithmic feeds, likes, or notifications, or simply boot any account suspected of belonging to someone under 18. Either way, all users, and especially young people across both states, risk being shut out of major online spaces as they exist today.

When young people lose accounts or get pushed into stripped-down experiences, they lose contact with friends, support groups, community organizing, local news, creative audiences, and ways to speak out on current issues. U.S. law has long recognized that people under 18 have their own constitutional rights to speak and receive information, and sweeping age gates directly interfere with those rights.

Sources indicate that at the same time, lawmakers often sell age-verification mandates as a way to rein in Big Tech, yet the opposite happens in practice. Megacorporations like Meta and Google have the resources to build expensive age-estimation systems and absorb steep fines (such as $50,000 per violation in California) while they figure out compliance. Smaller platforms and independent communities such as Bluesky or Dreamwidth, however, cannot afford those legal risks or engineering costs. As we have already seen in states like Mississippi, crushing compliance burdens push smaller sites out of the market and drive users back toward the biggest corporate giants. Instead of holding Big Tech accountable, these rules entrench its dominance; leaving everyone with fewer community options, less innovation, and a more centralized surveillance machine.

Legislative and regulatory action are setbacks, but they do not settle the debate. If these rules affect you in California, Newly introduced York, or anywhere else: keep a record while the details are still fresh, and share it with our team at agegates@eff.org.

Sources indicate that take screenshots and note the date, time, service, and what you were trying to do; write down what you lost (whether that means an account, a club or volunteer group, contact with friends, local news, or a favorite creator) or note if you chose to walk away from a service rather than submit an ID or personal data. You do not need to hand over sensitive information to show that these rules burdened you. If you hit an age check or parental-consent snag, save what the platform asked for, whether it worked or failed, any privacy promises or laws cited, and any appeal attempts.

If these restrictions get in your way, email EFF at agegates@eff.org and tell us what happened. Tracking real-world lockouts, age-check failures, and infringements on free speech puts us in a stronger position to challenge the worst of these restrictions in legislatures and the courts. At the same time, we will keep fighting for laws that actually make people safer online by curbing corporate surveillance and giving parents, youth, and all internet users meaningful choice and control.

While the organization made its name as a provider of orbital debuts utilizing reusable rocket technologies and its Starlink satellite-based communication services, AI has already become the biggest sales driver for the overall company.

Industry observers note that in the third quarter, SpaceX's super intelligence segment accounted for $7.56 billion of the organization's total $14.58 billion in revenue. While the large majority of the company's super intelligence reporting unit generates sales from artificial intelligence services, it also included roughly $538 million in advertising revenue primarily from the X social media platform in the quarter. Even after backing out the contribution from advertising, the super intelligence unit still accounted for roughly 48% total revenue in the quarter.

In a recent development, spaceX's super intelligence segment revenue increased 195% sequentially in the third quarter and was up 830% on an annual basis. With that kind of momentum, it's virtually certain that AI-derived sales will account for the majority of the company's overall revenue in this year's fourth quarter and going forward. Big contracts with Anthropic and Alphabet are primed to play big roles in driving that growth.

SpaceX has quickly become a powerhouse in the AI compute services category. The firm has a contract to provide $920 million a month in AI compute to Alphabet over a 33-month period, working out to a $30 billion deal. It also has a compute deal with Anthropic that's set to ramp up to its full value of $3.1 billion per month this December and potentially extend through 2029 -- working out to a max contract value of $120.5 billion. While the Anthropic deal includes guaranteed provisioning that expires in the first quarter and the option for either party to back out with a 90-day notice, the contract is effectively locked in for the period due to the notice requirements.

NASDAQ · As of 10:39 AM ET 11/27/26.

To put the significance of just the Anthropic deal in perspective, SpaceX has guided for its Q1 2027 revenue to come in between $33 billion and $37 billion. Meanwhile, that Anthropic service contract is set to deliver sales of $9.3 billion in the quarter -- representing 26.6% of revenue at the midpoint of the organization's guidance range. If you include the $2.76 billion in projected sales to Alphabet in the quarter, compute contracts with just those to customers account for 34.5% of SpaceX's midpoint revenue target for the period.

It has been revealed that if SpaceX manages to secure contract renewals from Anthropic and OpenAI, it would be a substantial bullish catalyst for the stock. AI has become the organization's most notable growth driver, and securing contract renewals would be a strong indicator for the company's competitive viability and long-term growth opportunities in the space. There are other factors that will affect the company's overall valuation, but AI has become central to the company's overall growth story -- and substantial contracts with Anthropic and Alphabet are at the heart.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sean Williams – Nov 27, 2026 at 5:06AM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Apple ›.

It's been a record-breaking year for Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA -0.04%)(BRKB +0.12%) in more ways than one. Despite Warren Buffett retiring as CEO at the end of last year, his successor, Greg Abel, has led the tech giant's shares to an all-time high.

Even though Abel completely overhauled Berkshire's $346 billion investment portfolio in the first quarter, one common thread between Berkshire's current and former bosses remains the same: portfolio concentration. Both Buffett and Abel strongly believe in wagering big on their best ideas. As of the closing bell on Nov. 20, 47% of Berkshire's invested assets ($162.6 billion) were put to work in three proven winners: Apple (AAPL +0.84%), American Express (AXP +1.18%), and Coca-Cola (KO -0.29%).

Recent findings suggest that greg Abel now oversees Berkshire's investment portfolio following Warren Buffett's retirement. Image source: Getty Images.

If there's a theme among all three of these stocks, it's that they were all built up by the Oracle of Omaha. Warren Buffett began buying shares of Apple in the first quarter of 2016, eventually building a nearly 944.3-million-share position at its peak in 2020.

Buffett's lure with Apple was its extremely loyal customer base and its exceptional pricing power.

NASDAQ · As of 10:40 AM ET 11/27/26.

Furthermore, Apple has executed the largest nominal share repurchase program on Wall Street. Through the end of Apple's fiscal 2026 (ending Sept. 26), the company has repurchased $902.8 billion of its common stock, retiring nearly 45% of its outstanding shares in the process.

But it's Apple's innovative prowess that entices Greg Abel. Under Tim Cook, who stepped down as CEO on Sept. 1, the company shifted to higher-margin subscription services and introduced its generative artificial intelligence (AI) platform, Apple Intelligence.

Credit-services provider American Express (Amex) is Berkshire Hathaway's second-longest holding (since 1991) and was labeled an "indefinite" position by Warren Buffett in his 2023 letter to shareholders.

NYSE · As of 10:37 AM ET 11/27/26.

Amex benefits from being cyclical and tackling both sides of the transaction counter. It's the third-largest payment processor in the U.S. by credit-card-network purchase volume, meaning it collects sizable merchant fees to facilitate transactions. It's also a lender, generating annual fees and interest income from its cardholders (businesses and individuals). Given that economic expansions last considerably longer than recessions, being able to double-dip works in Amex's favor more often than not.

Additionally, Amex has historically attracted well-to-do clientele. High earners are less likely to alter their spending habits or fail to pay their bills than the average-earning worker, allowing Amex to bounce back from economic downturns faster than most other lenders.

Industry observers note that no stock in Berkshire Hathaway's portfolio has been held longer than Coca-Cola (since 1988). Thanks to Berkshire's minuscule cost basis in Coca-Cola and the latter's 64-year streak of raising its dividend, Abel's company is netting a 65% annual yield on cost from this position.

According to recent reports, coca-Cola's long-term outperformance stems from its well-known brand name and global reach. With the exception of North Korea, Cuba, and Russia, it has operations in every country. This allows it to generate organic growth in emerging markets while reaping the steady reward of predictable operating cash flow in developed countries.

NYSE · As of 10:37 AM ET 11/27/26.

In a recent development, the argument can also be made that Coca-Cola's marketing is unrivaled. The company's holiday tie-ins, coupled with its use of AI in social media marketing campaigns, help it cross generational gaps and connect with consumers of all ages.

AI made self-hosting fun again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 155 min read (30987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Janlukas

⏱️ ~155 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been self-hosting things for many years.
  • I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with latest things.
  • Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting challenges. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more key than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.
